:::{#thm-zhz-sum-squares}
#### $\vecf{z}^{\mathsf{H}}\vecf{z}$ is a sum of squared absolute values

For every $\vecf{z} \in \mathbb{C}^p$,

$$\underbrace{\vecf{z}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{1 \times p}\,\underbrace{\vecf{z}}_{p \times 1} = \sumjp \abs{z_j}^2,$$

which is a nonnegative real number,
and is $0$ only when $\vecf{z} = \vzero_{p \times 1}$.

:::

::: proof

The last step uses the [identity for a complex number times its conjugate](algebra.qmd#thm-conj-product).

$$
\ba
\vecf{z}^{\mathsf{H}}\vecf{z}
&= \sumjp \overline{z_j}\,z_j
&& \text{(@def-conjugate-transpose, and the row-times-column product)}
\\
&= \sumjp z_j\,\overline{z_j}
&& \text{(complex multiplication is commutative)}
\\
&= \sumjp \abs{z_j}^2
&& \text{(a number times its conjugate)}
\ea
$$

By the definition of the [absolute value](algebra.qmd#def-complex-modulus),
each $\abs{z_j}^2 = (\operatorname{Re} z_j)^2 + (\operatorname{Im} z_j)^2$ is a nonnegative real number,
so their sum is too.
A sum of nonnegative numbers is $0$ only when every term is $0$,
and $\abs{z_j}^2 = 0$ only when

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Re} z_j &= \operatorname{Im} z_j \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
$$

that is, when $z_j = 0$.

:::
